text:
Condition: Atopic Dermatitis
Section: Overview

What Is It: Atopic dermatitis is the most common type of eczema. It is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by intensely itchy, dry, irritable, and inflamed skin. It follows a relapsing-remitting course characterized by acute flare-ups and periods of clearance.
How Common: Very common, especially in children; it most often begins early in life (between 2 months and 5 years of age). It can also start during puberty or adulthood.
Chronic Or Acute: Chronic condition that can last for years or be lifelong, although many children see their symptoms resolve by their teenage years.
Contagious: No
Skin Barrier Pathophysiology: The skin barrier (stratum corneum) functions like a protective brick wall. In atopic dermatitis, microscopic gaps form in this barrier, allowing excessive moisture to escape (causing profound dryness and xerosis) while permitting environmental irritants, allergens, and microbial pathogens (bacteria and viruses) to penetrate into deeper skin layers, driving inflammatory flares.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)
Page: (AAD)/Eczema types: Atopic dermatitis overview
Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/eczema/types/atopic-dermatitis

content.name: Intense Itching (Pruritus)
content.description: Described as 'the itch that rashes'. Itching is often severe, persistent, worsens at night, and disrupts sleep, contributing to fatigue, anxiety, and distress.
content.timing: Particularly aggravated at night, during sweating, or when exposed to dry cold air.

content.appearance: Pink/red rash on lighter skin or purplish/grayish/brown on darker skin; rough bumps, oozing lesions, and crusting caused by rubbing against bedding or carpeting.
content.behavioral_impact: Extreme restlessness, constant rubbing against sheets or caregivers, fussiness, and severe difficulty sleeping.

text:
Condition: Atopic Dermatitis
Section: Symptoms
Subsection: Age Variation - Infants and Babies (Under 2)

Typical Locations:
  - Cheeks and facial skin
  - Scalp and forehead
  - Outer arms and legs (extensor surfaces)
  - Trunk
Appearance: Pink/red rash on lighter skin or purplish/grayish/brown on darker skin; rough bumps, oozing lesions, and crusting caused by rubbing against bedding or carpeting.
Behavioral Impact: Extreme restlessness, constant rubbing against sheets or caregivers, fussiness, and severe difficulty sleeping.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

typical_locations: Front of knees and elbows (frequently observed in darker skin tones)
content.appearance: Itchy, scaly patches, discrete follicular papules (small itchy bumps), Dennie-Morgan folds (distinctive creases under lower eyelids), and areas of thickened skin from chronic scratching.

content.name: Dry Air and Low Humidity
content.threshold_risk: Relative humidity below 40% or sudden indoor/outdoor humidity drops
content.mechanism: Dries out the stratum corneum rapidly, widening skin barrier gaps, causing micro-cracking, severe tightness, and triggering intense itch receptors.
content.prevention_and_action: Use an indoor cool-mist humidifier in bedrooms and living spaces; apply thick ointment or cream emollients 2 to 3 times daily.

text:
Condition: Atopic Dermatitis
Section: Triggers
Subsection: Trigger

Id: trig_dry_air
Name: Dry Air and Low Humidity
Type: environmental
Weather Variable: relative_humidity
Threshold Risk: Relative humidity below 40% or sudden indoor/outdoor humidity drops
Mechanism: Dries out the stratum corneum rapidly, widening skin barrier gaps, causing micro-cracking, severe tightness, and triggering intense itch receptors.
Prevention And Action: Use an indoor cool-mist humidifier in bedrooms and living spaces; apply thick ointment or cream emollients 2 to 3 times daily.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)
Page: (AAD)/Childhood eczema: Triggers can cause eczema to flare
Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/eczema/childhood/triggers

content.name: Cold Temperatures and Artificial Indoor Heating
content.threshold_risk: Cold outdoor weather (< 10°C / 50°F) combined with dry forced-air heating
content.mechanism: Cold outdoor air combined with indoor radiators/heaters depletes atmospheric moisture and strips the natural lipid mantle of the skin.
content.prevention_and_action: Dress in soft breathable 100% cotton layers; apply a protective layer of barrier ointment before heading outdoors; keep indoor heating moderate.

Threshold Risk: Cold outdoor weather (< 10°C / 50°F) combined with dry forced-air heating
Mechanism: Cold outdoor air combined with indoor radiators/heaters depletes atmospheric moisture and strips the natural lipid mantle of the skin.
Prevention And Action: Dress in soft breathable 100% cotton layers; apply a protective layer of barrier ointment before heading outdoors; keep indoor heating moderate.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

content.name: High Heat and Sweating
content.threshold_risk: Warm/hot weather (> 28°C / 82°F) or heavy exertion causing active perspiration
content.mechanism: Sweat contains mineral salts and metabolic byproducts that directly irritate broken skin barrier, causing severe stinging and prickly itch.
content.prevention_and_action: Stay in cool or air-conditioned environments; take brief lukewarm or cool showers promptly after sweating; pat dry gently and reapply moisturizer.

Prevention And Action: Stay in cool or air-conditioned environments; take brief lukewarm or cool showers promptly after sweating; pat dry gently and reapply moisturizer.

content.name: Sudden Temperature Shifts
content.threshold_risk: Abrupt transitions between cold outdoor air and heated indoor rooms, or hot outdoors and icy air conditioning
content.mechanism: Rapid cutaneous vascular constriction and dilation combined with sudden moisture evaporation stimulates neurogenic itch pathways.
content.prevention_and_action: Layer clothing so layers can be added or removed gradually to adjust comfortably to ambient temperatures.

content.name: Fragrances and Scented Products
content.threshold_risk: Direct skin contact with perfumes, fragranced lotions, scented soaps, or 'unscented' masking products
content.mechanism: Aromatic chemicals penetrate disrupted skin barrier and act as primary irritants or trigger contact allergic sensitization.
content.prevention_and_action: Exclusively purchase products labeled 'Fragrance-Free'. Avoid products labeled 'Unscented' because they contain masking fragrances that can still flare eczema.

content.name: Harsh Soaps, Detergents, and Cleaning Chemicals
content.threshold_risk: Regular alkaline bar soaps, bubble baths, antibacterial washes, or standard laundry detergents
content.mechanism: Strong alkaline surfactants emulsify and dissolve the skin's protective lipid bilayer.
content.prevention_and_action: Use mild, soap-free, dye-free, and fragrance-free synthetic cleansers (syndet bars/liquids) and fragrance-free laundry detergents; double-rinse clothes.

content.name: Coarse Fabrics and Clothing Tags (Wool and Synthetics)
content.threshold_risk: Direct skin contact with wool sweaters, coarse polyester, nylon, or scratchy garment tags
content.mechanism: Mechanical friction and rigid fiber ends abrade sensitive stratum corneum.
content.prevention_and_action: Wear loose-fitting, soft 100% cotton clothing; remove clothing tags or choose tagless items; line irritating seams with silk; never wear wool next to bare skin.

content.name: Chlorinated Swimming Pool Water
content.threshold_risk: Swimming in chemically chlorinated pools or hot tubs
content.mechanism: Chlorine strips superficial moisture and natural oils from vulnerable skin.
content.prevention_and_action: Apply a barrier coat of petroleum jelly or thick ointment prior to swimming; shower with fresh warm water immediately upon exiting pool; apply moisturizer within 3 minutes.

content.threshold_risk: Psychological stress, exams, emotional strain, social distress
content.mechanism: Stress hormones (cortisol, catecholamines) and pro-inflammatory neuropeptides impair barrier recovery and intensify the itch-scratch cycle.

bathing_protocol: Take short baths or showers (5 to 10 minutes maximum) once daily or every other day.
Use lukewarm (warm) water, never hot water, as hot water strips away essential skin barrier oils.
Use mild, soap-free, fragrance-free cleanser only where needed (groin, armpits, feet, neck); do not scrub skin with washcloths or sponges.
Gently pat the skin dry with a clean, soft cotton towel—never rub vigorously.
moisturizing_protocol_soak_and_seal: Follow the 'Soak and Seal' method: Apply prescribed topical medicine and/or generous thick moisturizer within 3 minutes of stepping out of bath while skin is still slightly damp.
Select thick ointments (like petroleum jelly) or rich barrier creams rather than thin lotions, as lotions contain higher water and alcohol content that evaporate quickly and may irritate skin.
Reapply moisturizer whenever skin feels dry, tight, or itchy throughout the day (at least 2 to 3 times daily).
Only use products explicitly labeled 'Fragrance-Free'. Avoid 'Unscented' products.
patch_testing_new_products: Before applying any new moisturizer or skin product widely, apply a small (quarter-sized) amount to the inner arm daily for 7 to 10 consecutive days.
If the test spot shows no redness, rash, or itching after 10 days, the product is generally safe for broader use.
clothing_and_laundry_hygiene: Wear loose-fitting, breathable 100% cotton clothing, bed linens, and towels.
Avoid wool, mohair, and coarse synthetic fabrics directly against the skin.
Wash all newly purchased clothing and bedding before first use.
Use dye-free and fragrance-free liquid laundry detergent; avoid fabric softeners and dryer sheets.
Remove tags from clothing or buy tagless garments; cover irritating seams with silk.

text:
Condition: Atopic Dermatitis
Section: Skin Care and Self Care

Bathing Protocol:
  - Take short baths or showers (5 to 10 minutes maximum) once daily or every other day.
  - Use lukewarm (warm) water, never hot water, as hot water strips away essential skin barrier oils.
  - Use mild, soap-free, fragrance-free cleanser only where needed (groin, armpits, feet, neck); do not scrub skin with washcloths or sponges.
  - Gently pat the skin dry with a clean, soft cotton towel—never rub vigorously.
Moisturizing Protocol Soak And Seal:
  - Follow the 'Soak and Seal' method: Apply prescribed topical medicine and/or generous thick moisturizer within 3 minutes of stepping out of bath while skin is still slightly damp.
  - Select thick ointments (like petroleum jelly) or rich barrier creams rather than thin lotions, as lotions contain higher water and alcohol content that evaporate quickly and may irritate skin.
  - Reapply moisturizer whenever skin feels dry, tight, or itchy throughout the day (at least 2 to 3 times daily).
  - Only use products explicitly labeled 'Fragrance-Free'. Avoid 'Unscented' products.
Patch Testing New Products:
  - Before applying any new moisturizer or skin product widely, apply a small (quarter-sized) amount to the inner arm daily for 7 to 10 consecutive days.
  - If the test spot shows no redness, rash, or itching after 10 days, the product is generally safe for broader use.
Clothing And Laundry Hygiene:
  - Wear loose-fitting, breathable 100% cotton clothing, bed linens, and towels.
  - Avoid wool, mohair, and coarse synthetic fabrics directly against the skin.
  - Wash all newly purchased clothing and bedding before first use.
  - Use dye-free and fragrance-free liquid laundry detergent; avoid fabric softeners and dryer sheets.
  - Remove tags from clothing or buy tagless garments; cover irritating seams with silk.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

New or spreading patches of redness, warmth, or darker discoloration
Increased skin roughness, flaking, or tiny raised bumps
immediate_action_plan: Start prescribed topical anti-inflammatory treatment (such as topical corticosteroid, TCI, or crisaborole) at the earliest sign of flare as directed by dermatologist.

text:
Condition: Atopic Dermatitis
Section: Flare-Up Management

Early Signs Of Flare:
  - Localized increase in itching intensity or urge to scratch
  - New or spreading patches of redness, warmth, or darker discoloration
  - Increased skin roughness, flaking, or tiny raised bumps
  - Nocturnal awakenings caused by itching
Immediate Action Plan:
  - Start prescribed topical anti-inflammatory treatment (such as topical corticosteroid, TCI, or crisaborole) at the earliest sign of flare as directed by dermatologist.
  - Intensify skin barrier hydration by applying thick ointment-based moisturizers frequently.
  - Apply cool, damp cotton compresses to itchy areas for 10 to 15 minutes to quickly soothe inflammation.
  - Identify and eliminate any recently introduced triggers (e.g., weather changes, new detergent, sweating, chlorine).

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

content.sign: Eczema Herpeticum (Disseminated Herpes Simplex Virus Infection)
content.description: Sudden outbreak of numerous clustered, dome-shaped fluid-filled blisters or punched-out sores, accompanied by high fever, chills, fatigue, and swollen lymph glands.
content.urgency: Medical Emergency (Seek immediate emergency room or urgent care attention)
content.action: Potentially life-threatening, especially in infants and young children. Requires immediate systemic antiviral treatment (such as acyclovir).
